title: Patrick
hook: a British boy kidnapped to Ireland escapes, then goes back to the people who enslaved him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chalcedon, and your line was truly god, truly human. Whose view did you say back to them before your own? Day seven hundred eighty-four.

Raiders come to a family's land in Britain and carry off a boy, along with many others, across the sea to Ireland. He's put to work watching animals on the hills, alone, through rain and frost and snow. His father was a deacon, his grandfather a priest, and the boy, by his own account, had paid none of it much attention. Now, out on the hillside, he starts to pray. Years later he'll write the story himself, in rough Latin he apologizes for. Today: Patrick.

Patrick's Confession doesn't read like a legend. It reads like a man explaining his life to people who doubted him. On that hillside, he says, the love of God grew in him. He prayed through the day and into the night, in snow and frost and rain, and felt no harm. Then one night, in his sleep, he heard a voice: your ship is ready. He ran, a long way, he says, to a coast he didn't know, talked his way onto a ship, and after hard days, and some years, was home with his family again. His family begged him never to leave them again. Then came another dream. A man named Victoricus seemed to come from Ireland, carrying letters, more than could be counted. He handed one over, and at the top it said: The Voice of the Irish. As Patrick read, he heard the people from beside the western sea calling to him, as if with one voice: holy boy, we beg you, come and walk among us again. And he went back. To the land where he'd been a slave. To the people who had taken him. As a bishop he baptized and ordained, and he refused gifts, even handing back what was left on the altar, so no one could say he'd come for profit. It wasn't safe. He writes of being seized and put in chains. Jesus had said, in the King James: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." Patrick doesn't cast himself as the hero. He calls himself a sinner, the least of the faithful, and gives the credit to God. The shamrock and the snakes come from later stories, not from his own pages. What his pages hold is stranger: a man who went back.
screen: `BACK TO THE PEOPLE WHO TOOK HIM.`
`NO SHAMROCK: A MAN WHO WENT BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go back, gently, to a place of hurt, carrying something good. Settle, and breathe. Let a place or a person tied to an old hurt come to mind. Not the deepest one; something you can hold today. And stay safe: going back in your heart never means walking back into harm. Ask one small question. Is there a good thing I could bring there now? A kind word. A visit. Simply wishing them well, from a distance. If you pray, you can bring that place to God. If you don't, hold it in steady goodwill for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Patrick. The captive who escaped, then heard the voice of the Irish and went back. That ends a week of Jerome, the pears, Ostia, Rome, the golden mouth, Chalcedon and Patrick.
Your line: the voice of the irish. Today, think of someone you'd rather not go back to, and, if it's safe, do one small good thing in their direction. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox and other Christians honor Patrick as a saint and the apostle of Ireland; his Confession is read as his own account of his captivity, escape and return.

notes: No age or numbers stated (Confession 1 gives 'about sixteen' and 'many thousands'; the script says 'along with many others'). Father Calpornius a deacon, grandfather Potitus a priest (Confession 1); names omitted. Confirm.
Confession 16–17: prayer on the hills in snow, frost and rain; the voice 'your ship is ready'; the long flight to the coast. Paraphrased.

Confession 23: Victoricus, 'innumerable letters', 'Vox Hiberionacum', the voices by the wood of Foclut near the western sea: 'we ask thee, holy youth, to come and walk among us once more'. Paraphrased; please confirm the Latin spelling and pronunciation in the original game.
Confession 49–52: returning gifts left on the altar; being seized and put in irons. Confirm.
Shamrock and snakes: from later hagiography and folklore, not in the Confession. Week-end look-back in the word segment covers days 778–784.
Editor: 'never casts himself' softened to 'doesn't cast himself' (no absolute claim).
Editor 2: escape compressed less (Confession 23 has him home 'after a few years', not straight after the voyage); practice opener varied.
